This can be the case even when I have myself experienced the situation, because I find that others have experienced it differently in ways I could not guess. Interviewing is our only defense against mistaken expectations. Anyone entering a new conceptual area should make every effort to obtain, early in the study, images and ideas based on experience rather than surmise. As soon as possible, the investigator should conduct pilot interviews.

几乎在我开展的每一项新研究中，我都会惊喜地发现，事情的发展往往出乎我的意料，却又恰恰符合预期。即便我自己也经历过类似情况，这种情况也可能发生，因为我发现其他人对同一件事的体验与我预想的截然不同。访谈是我们避免错误预期的唯一途径。任何进入全新概念领域的人都应该尽一切努力，在研究初期就基于经验而非臆测来获取图像和想法。研究者应尽快开展试点访谈。

Just because initial expectations are so likely to be inaccurate, interview guides for pilot interviews can be largely misdirected. Areas asked about can turn out to be dull and unproductive while areas not included in the guide turn out to be critical. The interviewer, especially in the first pilot interview, may experience bad patches, where it is hard to make connection with the respondent and hard to know how to proceed. However, after only a first or second interview, the way things are begins to fall into place. Eventually, it will be obvious what is important; initially, it rarely is.

正因为最初的预期很可能不准确，试点访谈的访谈指南也可能造成很大的误导。指南中提及的话题可能枯燥乏味、毫无成效，而指南中未涵盖的内容却至关重要。访谈者，尤其是在第一次试点访谈中，可能会遇到一些棘手的问题，例如难以与受访者建立联系，也难以把握访谈的走向。然而，通常经过一两次访谈后，情况就会逐渐明朗起来。最终，哪些内容真正重要会变得显而易见；但在最初阶段，这一点往往并不明显。

One implication of these observations is that pilot interviews are highly desirable. Another is that even when interviewing for the study proper starts, interview guides should be seen as provisional and likely to change as more is learned. In a study of a representative sample, where the same guide is to be used with the entire sample, the guide may not stabilize until the fourth or fifth pilot interview. Even then the guide may undergo further modification as the study develops. In my study of wellfunctioning men it wasn’t until we were halfway into our interviewing that I realized we weren’t learning nearly enough about marital quarrels and other problems of personal life.

这些观察结果的一个启示是，试访谈非常必要。另一个启示是，即使正式研究的访谈开始后，访谈指南也应被视为暂定版本，并可能随着研究进展而进行调整。在针对代表性样本的研究中，如果所有样本都使用同一份指南，那么指南可能要到第四或第五次试访谈后才能最终定型。即便如此，随着研究的进行，指南仍可能需要进一步修改。在我针对身心健康男性的研究中，直到访谈进行到一半时，我才意识到我们对婚姻争吵和其他个人生活问题的了解远远不够。

Just as interview guides take a while to stabilize, so too can research aims. Every funding agency requires that investigators know what they are after and be able to list the aims of the study in their proposals. Sometimes there are indeed specific questions the investigator hopes to answer. Yet it is often the case that the investigator knows only that the area of study is attractive, possibly because it is important and yet murky, possessed of mysteries. It is as though the area dares the investigator to discover what is going on. You couldn’t very well write that into a research proposal.

就像访谈提纲需要一段时间才能定型一样，研究目标也需要时间酝酿。每个资助机构都要求研究人员清楚自己的研究方向，并能在研究计划书中列出研究目标。有时，研究人员确实希望解答一些具体问题。然而，很多时候，研究人员只知道某个研究领域很有吸引力，或许是因为它既重要又晦涩难懂，充满了谜团。仿佛这个领域在挑战研究人员去探索其中的奥秘。你不可能把这些都写进研究计划书中。

When the investigator’s reason for undertaking a study is not much more than a belief that a situation is intriguing and worth studying, one of the problems of the research enterprise will be to find the research problem that justifies the research. Findings and problem may emerge together. An investigator’s initial aim in a qualitative interview study of blue-collar marriages might be simply to know more about blue-collar marriages. Eventually, the investigator might be able to define the study’s aim as learning what happens in situations where the husband’s ability to provide an income, and in this way to be a reliable husband and father, is always in question. There must be some aim for the study to begin, but sometimes it is only toward the end of a study that its focus becomes well defined. 6

当研究者开展一项研究的理由仅仅是认为某个情况引人入胜且值得研究时，研究工作面临的难题之一就是找到能够证明研究合理性的研究问题。研究结果和问题可能同时出现。例如，在对蓝领婚姻进行定性访谈研究中，研究者的最初目标可能仅仅是想更多地了解蓝领婚姻。最终，研究者或许能够将研究目标定义为：了解在丈夫的收入能力（从而能否成为一个可靠的丈夫和父亲）始终受到质疑的情况下，会发生什么。研究必须有目标才能开始，但有时只有在研究接近尾声时，其关注点才会变得清晰明确。

TO TAPE OR NOT TO TAPE

贴胶带还是不贴胶带

Investigators’ policies regarding the use of tape recorders vary enormously. At one extreme is the investigator whose books are compilations of interview excerpts, who brings two tape recorders to an interview, each with its lapel mike, clips each mike on the respondent’s shirt front, and sets both machines going. At the other extreme are investigators who treat a tape recorder as an intruder in the interview.

调查人员在使用录音机方面的做法差异巨大。一种极端情况是，有些调查人员的记录册是访谈摘录的汇编，他们会携带两台录音机进行访谈，每台录音机都配有领夹式麦克风，将麦克风分别夹在受访者的衬衫前襟上，然后启动两台机器。另一种极端情况是，有些调查人员将录音机视为访谈中的干扰物。

Tape recorders remind people that there will be a record of what they say. Even when people seem to have stopped attending to the tape recorder they can feel constrained by its presence. Most experienced qualitative interviewers have had a respondent who, upon using a word that is obscene or vulgar, turned to the tape recorder to apologize to the transcriber. And almost every qualitative interviewer has had a respondent who hesitated before sharing a confidence and then said something like “Would you mind turning off the tape recorder, because there is something I want to tell you I don’t want to have on the tape?”

录音机时刻提醒人们，他们所说的话会被记录下来。即使人们似乎不再关注录音机，它的存在仍然会让他们感到束缚。大多数经验丰富的定性访谈者都遇到过这样的情况：受访者在说了不雅或粗俗的词语后，会转向录音机向转录员道歉。几乎每位定性访谈者都遇到过这样的情况：受访者在分享秘密之前犹豫片刻，然后说：“您介意把录音机关掉吗？因为有些话我想告诉您，但我不想被录下来。”

And what do you do with the tapes when you’ve got them? They take hours to transcribe, and then you find that the important material is hidden in the paragraphs and pages of verbiage. Nor do you really need it all. Some first-rate investigators insist that they can remember enough after an interview to write an adequate report. 7 And one investigator I know believes that there is a useful discipline in taking notes. A tape recorder, she believes, encourages you to let your mind wander because you know the recorder will capture what the respondent is saying; note taking requires you to focus.

那么，拿到录音带之后该怎么办呢？转录录音带要花好几个小时，而且你会发现重要的内容都隐藏在冗长的文字段落和页面中。你也并不需要全部内容。一些一流的调查员坚持认为，他们每次访谈后都能记住足够多的信息来撰写一份合格的报告。我认识的一位调查员认为，做笔记是一种很有用的习惯。她认为，录音机会让你放任思绪游离，因为你知道录音机会自动记录受访者所说的话；而做笔记则需要你集中注意力。

My experience is different. I find that using a tape recorder makes it easier for me to attend to the respondent than when I take notes, just because I don’t have to worry about getting down all the respondent’s words. (To be sure, I am sometimes instead distracted by worry that the recorder has failed.)

我的经验有所不同。我发现使用录音机比做笔记更容易让我集中注意力倾听受访者，因为我不用担心记不住受访者说的所有话。（当然，有时我反而会因为担心录音机出故障而分心。）

But most important to people who tape-record is that notes never capture exactly what was said. Note taking tends to simplify and flatten respondents’ speech patterns. The conversational spacers (“You know what I mean?”) are dropped in note taking; so are respondents’ false starts and stray thoughts and parenthetic remarks. The vividness of speech disappears.

但对录音者来说，最重要的是笔记永远无法准确记录谈话内容。记笔记往往会简化和抹平受访者的说话方式。谈话中的停顿语（比如“你明白我的意思吗？”）在记笔记时会被省略；受访者的语塞、零散的想法和插入语也会被忽略。生动的语言表达就此消失。

Content is likely to be lost as well. While I have a fairly good shorthand for a nonstenographer, when I try to take verbatim notes I regularly omit the unimportant and much of the parenthetic (“I shouldn’t be telling you this, but …”). Often, I am also forced to omit detail. Suppose a retiree is describing a morning routine: “I get up earlier than my wife and go down to start breakfast and then put it on a tray and bring it upstairs. And we just sit in bed talking and having breakfast and reading the paper and my wife will start the crossword …” If this is given to me rapidly and I am taking notes, I will get down the very first words but will surely miss a good part of what follows. Indeed, if a respondent is speaking rapidly, I will often have to skip material to keep up.

内容也可能因此丢失。虽然我作为一个非速记员，速记能力还算不错，但当我尝试逐字记录时，我经常会省略一些不重要的内容和大量的括号内信息（“我不应该告诉你这些，但是……”）。很多时候，我也不得不省略一些细节。假设一位退休人士正在描述他的晨间日常：“我比妻子起得早，下楼准备早餐，然后放在托盘上端到楼上。我们坐在床上边吃早餐边聊天、看报纸，我妻子会开始做填字游戏……”如果他语速很快，而我又在做笔记，我只能记下开头几个字，肯定会错过后面的大部分内容。事实上，如果受访者语速很快，我常常不得不跳过一些内容才能跟上。

I now regularly tape-record. 8 I do this because I am accustomed to working from verbatim transcripts and value the fidelity of the transcripts of tape-recorded material. I also value being spared the drudgery of transcribing shorthand notes. I began doing qualitative interviews before portable tape recorders were in general use, and I have done more than my share of transcribing shorthand notes into a typewriter or desk tape recorder. It is a time-consuming and wearing job. Although my shorthand has improved, I wouldn’t want to have to do all that transcription again.

我现在经常录音。我这样做是因为我习惯于根据逐字稿工作，并且重视录音资料转录的准确性。我也希望免去转录速记笔记的繁琐工作。在便携式录音机普及之前，我就开始进行定性访谈，也因此做了大量的速记笔记转录工作，要么用打字机，要么用台式录音机。这是一项耗时耗力的工作。虽然我的速记水平有所提高，但我不想再做一遍那样的转录工作了。

Whether to tape-record or not depends on what you intend doing with the interview material. If you want verbatim transcript, because you intend to quote respondents’ comments in your report, then you should make every effort to use a tape recorder. You will very likely later edit what the respondent said, but you will have control of the editing. Note taking enmeshes editing and recording and leaves you with no way to know what changes you have made in the respondent’s actual comments.

是否录音取决于您打算如何使用访谈资料。如果您需要逐字稿，因为您打算在报告中引用受访者的评论，那么您应该尽一切可能使用录音机。您之后很可能会编辑受访者的发言，但您可以控制编辑过程。而记笔记则会将编辑和录音混为一谈，让您无法了解自己对受访者实际发言做了哪些改动。

You should also consider tape recording if you want not so much to learn about events as to capture how a respondent saw them or reacted to them. Then the nuances and complexities of speech that are likely to be missed in note taking may be important for you. And certainly if you want a record of what was said because your version may some day be questioned, you would do well to use a tape recorder.

如果您并非想要了解事件本身，而是想记录受访者如何看待或应对事件，那么您也应该考虑录音。在这种情况下，笔记中容易忽略的言语细微差别和复杂之处可能对您至关重要。当然，如果您希望保留谈话记录，以防将来有人质疑您的说法，那么使用录音机也是明智之举。

But if all you want are facts and you don’t care about phrasings, you may be better off with notes. And if a tape recorder would be intrusive, then of course you should take notes and let the tape recorder go. For example, a study of how small entrepreneurs organize their business, where there is no anticipation of writing a report using quotations and where the respondents might be put off by a tape recorder, would be better done from notes.

但如果你只想要事实，并不在意措辞，那么记笔记或许更合适。如果录音会打扰到受访者，那么当然应该记笔记，而不要使用录音机。例如，一项关于小型企业主如何组织业务的研究，如果不需要撰写包含引语的报告，而且受访者可能对录音机感到不适，那么记笔记会是更好的选择。

Tape recorders can be, for some people in some circumstances, deterrents to candor. If your study requires you to learn things about people that could discredit them—let alone get them indicted—forget about using a tape recorder. Indeed, if you want to learn about actionable mistakes at work (such as the kinds of errors by physicians that would make them vulnerable to malpractice suits), even taking notes can put respondents off. You might do best, should you enter such an area of study, to slow your note taking and instead try to remember what you’re being told—and then write down as much of it as you can immediately after leaving the interview. 9

在某些情况下，录音机对某些人来说可能会阻碍他们坦诚相待。如果你的研究需要你了解一些可能损害他人名誉——更不用说可能让他们被起诉——的事情，那就别用录音机了。事实上，如果你想了解工作中可能造成实际后果的错误（例如医生可能因哪些错误而面临医疗事故诉讼），即使是做笔记也可能让受访者感到不自在。如果你真的要研究这类问题，最好的办法或许是放慢记笔记的速度，先努力记住受访者所说的话，然后在访谈结束后立即尽可能多地记录下来。

TRANSCRIPTION

转录

If you do tape-record, you must decide how much you will transcribe. Only as much as you need, of course, but how much is that? And how can you know whether you will need something until you see it?

如果你要录音，就必须决定要转录多少内容。当然，只转录你需要的量，但到底需要多少呢？而且，在看到录音之前，你怎么知道自己是否需要它呢？

One approach is to transcribe everything and use the transcripts as a set of materials to be mined, accepting that a good deal will be dross. This approach puts the analyst’s convenience before the time and money required for the transcription, and in an ambitious, well-funded study it is the way to go.

一种方法是将所有内容转录成文本，并将这些转录文本作为待挖掘的素材，但同时也要意识到其中很多内容可能毫无价值。这种方法将分析人员的便利置于转录所需的时间和金钱之上，对于一项雄心勃勃、资金充足的研究而言，这不失为一种可行的方法。

If a study’s budget is limited, consideration might be given to listening to a tape once, transcribing only what seems likely to be useful and paraphrasing the rest or noting something like “From minute 24 through 29 discussion of relationship with boss.” Another approach is to take notes on what is contained on the tape, never transcribing at all except for quotations to be used in the report. Still another approach is to take notes during the interview even though it is also being tape-recorded. The notes, when typed, can provide an index to the tape, and transcription can be done as needed.

如果研究预算有限，可以考虑只听一遍录音，只转录那些可能有用的内容，其余部分用自己的话复述，或者做个简短的记录，比如“从第24分钟到第29分钟，讨论了与老板的关系”。另一种方法是记录录音内容，除了报告中要引用的段落外，其他部分都不转录。还有一种方法是在访谈过程中边听边做笔记。把笔记整理成文字后，就可以作为录音的索引，需要时再进行转录。

Not long ago I participated in a study whose budget was too tight to fund the costs of transcription of interviews, let alone the travel costs of face-to-face interviews with respondents spread across the country. The aim of the study was to diagnose the source of a malaise within a national organization and to prescribe its remedy. I conducted taped telephone interviews with half a dozen organization members. I took sketchy notes on the interviews but did not transcribe any of the tapes. While writing my part of the report I listened to a couple of the tapes to remind myself of their contents and also drew from them a few telling quotations. Mostly, I relied on what I had learned while conducting the interviews and could consult my notes to be reminded of the remainder.

不久前，我参与了一项研究，该研究预算非常紧张，甚至连访谈录音的转录费用都难以承担，更遑论与分布在全国各地的受访者进行面对面访谈的差旅费了。这项研究旨在诊断一个全国性组织内部问题的根源并提出解决方案。我与该组织的六位成员进行了电话访谈，并进行了录音。我做了简单的笔记，但没有转录任何录音。在撰写报告时，我听了几段录音，以回忆访谈内容，并从中摘录了一些有见地的引语。大部分内容，我主要依靠访谈过程中了解到的信息，其余部分则可以参考笔记来回忆。

As in so much else in qualitative interview studies, there is no single right way. Everything depends on what is to be accomplished, the level of resources, and the nature of constraints.

就像定性访谈研究中的许多其他方面一样，并没有唯一正确的方法。一切都取决于要达成的目标、资源水平以及限制条件的性质。

HOW LONG SHOULD AN INTERVIEW LAST?

面试应该持续多久？

Most survey studies try to keep interviews to an hour or less. But qualitative interviews can run as long as 8 hours—with breaks, of course. If the interview is easy and sustaining, the respondent interested and cooperative, and the material instructive, and if there are no time constraints, a reasonable expectation is that the interview will go for an hour and a half or 2 hours. I do not often observe respondents getting tired or restless at the 2-hour point unless something has gone wrong in the interview. I may be tired, but respondents seem more often to be enlivened.

大多数调查研究都力求将访谈时间控制在一小时或更短。但定性访谈可能会持续长达八小时——当然，期间会有休息。如果访谈轻松且富有成效，受访者兴趣浓厚且配合，访谈内容富有启发性，且没有时间限制，那么访谈通常会持续一个半小时到两个小时。除非访谈过程中出现了问题，否则我很少观察到受访者在两个小时后感到疲倦或烦躁。我可能会感到疲倦，但受访者似乎往往精神焕发。

If there is tension in the interview because the respondent is ambivalent about being interviewed, then holding the interview to an hour might be right. If you don’t know what to anticipate, you might ask respondents to plan on an hour and a half, with the option of ending earlier or going on for a bit. Half an hour seems about the minimum time for an interview. Although any interchange, no matter how brief, can produce an interesting observation, I find it difficult to develop a coherent account in an interview of under half an hour.

如果受访者对接受采访感到犹豫不决，导致访谈气氛紧张，那么将访谈时间控制在一个小时以内或许比较合适。如果您不确定访谈会如何进行，可以请受访者预留一个半小时的时间，并允许他们选择提前结束或延长一些时间。半小时似乎是访谈的最短时长。虽然任何交流，无论多么简短，都可能产生有趣的见解，但我发现，在不到半小时的访谈中，很难形成连贯的叙述。

Once in a while a respondent seems willing to go on longer than I am. I believe it is good policy to support the fullest report a respondent can give and to continue an interview as long as it is productive. Nevertheless, interviewing can be wearing, and I can only do it for so long. When I become too tired to be fully in touch with what I am being told and it is possible for me to schedule another interview, I call a halt and make another appointment. But if the respondent lives far from me, and I’m not up for another two-hour drive out and two-hour drive back, or if there is no possibility of rescheduling, I’ll stay with an interview as long as there is material to cover.

偶尔，受访者似乎愿意比我更长时间地进行访谈。我认为，支持受访者尽可能提供完整报告，并在访谈富有成效的情况下继续进行，是合理的做法。然而，访谈会让人疲惫，我的能力也有限。当我感到疲惫不堪，无法完全理解受访者所说的话，并且有可能安排下一次访谈时，我会结束访谈并另约时间。但如果受访者住得很远，我不愿意再花两个小时开车往返，或者无法重新安排时间，那么只要还有内容需要探讨，我就会继续进行访谈。

HOW MANY INTERVIEWS WITH THE SAME RESPONDENT?

对同一受访者进行了多少次访谈？

It is almost always desirable, if time and costs permit, to interview respondents more than once. You have to keep your frame pretty narrow if you plan to cover it all in a single sitting. Furthermore, a first meeting is partly about establishing the research partnership. Interviewer and respondent get to know each other, get a sense of the rhythm of interchange, and establish the outlines of the respondent’s story. When they meet again they know each other better. Also, in the intervening time the respondent may have begun thinking about the areas discussed, and memories may have surfaced. Or the respondent may have been made more sensitive to the issues of the interview and may therefore have newly noted incidents worth reporting.

如果时间和成本允许，多次访谈受访者几乎总是可取的。如果您计划一次性完成所有访谈，则必须将访谈范围控制得非常窄。此外，初次访谈的部分目的在于建立研究伙伴关系。访谈者和受访者可以互相了解，熟悉交流节奏，并大致了解受访者的故事。下次访谈时，他们对彼此的了解会更加深入。同时，在此期间，受访者可能已经开始思考之前讨论过的话题，一些记忆可能会浮现。或者，受访者可能对访谈中涉及的问题更加敏感，因此可能会注意到一些值得记录的新事件。

With increasing contact and increasing confidence in the research procedure respondents are likely to be more willing to report fully. In the study of occupationally successful men it was only in a fourth interview that a respondent talked about his wife’s alcoholism. In a study of women who were single parents, where we interviewed a small sample every 2 weeks for about 5 months, we normally did not learn about the emotional ups and downs in relationships with boyfriends until the fifth or sixth interview.

随着接触增多和对研究程序信心的增强，受访者可能更愿意提供完整信息。在一项针对事业成功的男性的研究中，直到第四次访谈，才有一位受访者谈到他妻子的酗酒问题。在另一项针对单亲母亲的研究中，我们每两周对一小部分受访者进行一次访谈，持续约五个月，通常直到第五次或第六次访谈，我们才能了解到她们与男友关系中的情绪波动。

Only infrequently does the cost of a second interview with a respondent outweigh its usefulness. Third interviews are generally also worth doing. Of importance here is the number of areas to be covered in the interviewing. Fourth and fifth interviews are likely to produce a sense of diminishing returns, except when they provide information on continuing stories in respondents’ lives. It is not that nothing at all is learned from fourth or subsequent interviews; respondents can always report on new events or new aspects of already described events. The question is whether the investigator might not gain more by interviewing additional respondents.

只有极少数情况下，对受访者进行第二次访谈的成本才会超过其带来的益处。第三次访谈通常也是值得进行的。这里重要的是访谈需要涵盖的领域数量。第四次和第五次访谈可能会带来收益递减的感觉，除非它们能够提供受访者生活中持续发展的信息。这并不是说从第四次或之后的访谈中完全一无所获；受访者总能提供新的事件或已描述事件的新方面。问题在于，研究者是否可以通过访谈更多受访者获得更多信息。

Sometimes it is desirable to interview a few respondents many times but most respondents only a few times. That can provide the study with both extensive case reports and a reasonable sample size.

有时需要对少数受访者进行多次访谈，而对大多数受访者进行几次访谈。这样既能为研究提供丰富的案例报告，又能保证合理的样本量。

DO YOU PAY RESPONDENTS?

你们会向受访者支付报酬吗？

Some funded studies now pay respondents for their time. A New York City study of drug users, for example, paid respondents twenty-five dollars plus two subway tokens for completed interviews. My impression is that with very low income respondents the opportunity for payment can be an important incentive for participating in a study.

现在有些资助研究会向受访者支付报酬。例如，纽约市一项针对吸毒者的研究，就向完成访谈的受访者支付25美元外加两枚地铁代币。我的感觉是，对于收入非常低的受访者来说，报酬可以成为他们参与研究的重要激励因素。

In a study with middle-income respondents we acknowledged the contribution respondents made to the study by giving them a gift certificate to a restaurant after our first interview. Most were pleased and it may have aided rapport when we returned for further interviews, but I doubt that it was necessary for us to have done this.

在一项针对中等收入受访者的研究中，我们在第一次访谈后赠送受访者餐厅礼券，以感谢他们对研究的贡献。大多数受访者表示满意，这或许有助于我们在后续访谈中建立融洽的关系，但我认为我们没有必要这样做。

My guess is that in most studies the reward for a respondent is the interview itself and the contribution he or she can make to the study. Payment doesn’t seem to make a difference in a respondent’s willingness to participate. If the interview goes well, payment is largely irrelevant to the respondent’s experience, except for those who truly need the money; if it doesn’t go well, payment won’t make the experience better. Still, a gift to acknowledge a respondent’s contribution is likely to be appreciated.

我猜想，在大多数研究中，受访者的回报就是访谈本身以及他们能为研究做出的贡献。报酬似乎并不会影响受访者的参与意愿。如果访谈进行得很顺利，报酬对受访者的体验基本无关紧要，除非他们真的需要这笔钱；如果访谈不顺利，报酬也不会改善他们的体验。不过，一份小礼物来感谢受访者的贡献，他们很可能会感到欣慰。

WHERE DO YOU HOLD THE INTERVIEW?

面试地点在哪里？

An argument can be made for interviewing people in the investigator’s office: if you interview people in their home you’re not going to hear much that is inconsistent with their commitment to their home roles and if you interview people in their offices they are less likely to discuss problems with coworkers. Since most people seem to prefer your coming to them, most of my interviewing has been in respondents’ homes. Some investigators think that’s fine; they can observe the setting within which the respondent lives, may meet members of the respondent’s family, and may observe the respondent in interaction with them.

有人认为在调查员办公室进行访谈有其优势：如果在受访者家中访谈，他们不太可能谈及与家庭角色不符的内容；如果在办公室访谈，他们则不太可能谈及与同事之间的问题。由于大多数人似乎更倾向于调查员上门，因此我的大部分访谈都是在受访者家中进行的。一些调查员认为这种做法也无妨；他们可以观察受访者的生活环境，有机会见到受访者的家人，并观察受访者与家人的互动。

On the rarest of occasions the safety of interviewers may come into question. Interviewing respondents within their homes can pose a slight but nevertheless real risk, perhaps especially for women. I have told people who have interviewed for me to trust their intuitions, and to end the interview if they feel uneasy. Once a woman who was interviewing for me did not want to return for a second interview with a male respondent. She had no special reason; she just hadn’t felt comfortable with him. That feeling of discomfort was enough to go on. She may have been responding to minimal cues she was not able to identify, or she may have developed a sense of the respondent that told her the situation was dangerous. We found a male interviewer to take over for her.

在极少数情况下，访谈员的安全可能会受到威胁。在受访者家中进行访谈可能存在轻微但真实存在的风险，尤其对于女性而言。我曾告诉接受过我访谈的人员，要相信自己的直觉，如果感到不安，就应该结束访谈。曾经有一位女性受访者不想再和一位男性受访者进行第二次访谈。她并没有什么特别的理由，只是觉得和这位男性受访者相处不自在。这种不适感足以让她继续下去。她或许是对一些自己无法察觉的细微线索做出了反应，又或许她对这位受访者产生了一种预感，觉得情况很危险。我们最终找到了一位男性访谈员接替了她的工作。

With few exceptions, however, respondents who have agreed to be interviewed in their homes will go to some effort to be hospitable. Indeed, by far the most common response to a stranger within one’s home is friendly interest and desire to be of help.

然而，除少数例外情况外，同意接受上门采访的受访者都会尽力热情款待。事实上，对于家中来访的陌生人，最常见的反应莫过于友好的兴趣和乐于助人的意愿。

TELEPHONE INTERVIEWS

电话采访

Reasons of economy may make it seem desirable to interview by telephone. I have conducted many telephone interviews and regularly find that useful information can be developed. It helps for me to have met the respondent or at least to be able to identify myself with a project the respondent recognizes, so that the respondent knows I am who I purport to be. But even with my identity established, I don’t feel as much in touch with the respondent in a telephone interview as I do in a face-to-face interview. My shallower connection to the respondent generally produces a shorter interview. In one study in which I did both face-to-face interviews and telephone interviews, the face-to-face interviews ran an hour and a half or more, while the telephone interviews ran about 45 minutes, and sometimes less.

出于经济考虑，电话访谈似乎更可取。我进行过多次电话访谈，经常发现也能从中获得有用的信息。如果我事先见过受访者，或者至少能与受访者认可的项目建立联系，让受访者确信我就是本人，这对我很有帮助。但即便如此，在电话访谈中，我与受访者的联系仍然不如面对面访谈那样紧密。这种联系的浅薄通常会导致访谈时间更短。在我进行的一项研究中，我同时采用了面对面访谈和电话访谈，结果显示面对面访谈持续了一个半小时或更久，而电话访谈则只需大约45分钟，有时甚至更短。

A research project that compared telephone and face-to-face interviewing found that telephone respondents broke off contact more quickly, were both more acquiescent and more evasive, and were more cautious about self-revelation. 10 But a team that has done a great deal of telephone interviewing describes it as “the next best thing to being there.” 11 This strikes me as right: it’s better to be there, but telephone interviews are the next best thing.

一项比较电话访谈和面对面访谈的研究发现，电话受访者更容易中断联系，既更顺从也更回避问题，并且在自我披露方面更加谨慎。但一个进行过大量电话访谈的团队将其描述为“仅次于亲临现场的最佳方式”。我认为这很正确：亲临现场当然更好，但电话访谈是次佳选择。

# ↩

CHAPTER 4
INTERVIEWING

第四章 访谈

GETTING STARTED

入门

You have called the respondent to confirm that you are expected. You have checked your tape recorder. You have put your interview guide, fastened onto a clipboard, in your briefcase, first glancing at it to remind yourself of the interview’s aims and content. You get in your car, a street map beside you. You find the respondent’s home, park, ring the doorbell. The respondent comes to the door. You introduce yourself and are directed to a place to sit.

你已致电受访者确认他们会接待你。你检查了录音机。你把夹在写字板上的访谈指南放进公文包，事先快速浏览了一遍，提醒自己访谈的目的和内容。你上了车，旁边放着一张街道地图。你找到受访者的家，停车，按响门铃。受访者来开门。你做了自我介绍，并被引导到座位上坐下。

Your first concern should be to establish a good interviewing partnership. The way you act and what you say should communicate that you expect to work with the respondent to produce the interview. For example, as you bring out your tape recorder, you might ask, “Is using the tape recorder okay?” The point isn’t the particular remark but, rather, the assumption of a collaborative relationship.

你的首要任务应该是建立良好的访谈合作关系。你的言行举止应该传达出你希望与受访者合作完成访谈的信息。例如，当你拿出录音机时，你可以问：“可以使用录音机吗？” 重点不在于这句话本身，而在于你假定存在合作关系。

I bring two signed copies of a consent form to interviews. I give both to the respondent and say, “These are two copies of our consent form. Could you read one of them, and if it is all right would you sign it and give it to me and then hang on to the other?” Then I ask something like “Is there anything about the study you would like me to tell you before we begin?” Sometimes respondents want to know how they happened to be contacted. I then describe the sampling procedure. I almost always also say something about the general goal of the study, such as “We’re trying to learn about the experience of retirement and so are talking to people who know about it because they’re doing it.” I usually name the study’s sponsor or give my academic affiliation to provide additional evidence that the study is legitimate.

我每次访谈都会带两份签字的知情同意书。我会把两份都交给受访者，并说：“这是我们的两份知情同意书。您能读一下其中一份吗？如果可以的话，请您签字后交给我，另一份请您自己保管好。” 然后我会问一些类似“在访谈开始之前，您有什么想让我告诉您的吗？”之类的问题。有时受访者会想知道他们是如何被联系上的。这时我会解释一下抽样方法。我几乎总是会提及研究的总体目标，例如“我们正在努力了解退休生活，所以我们采访的是那些正在退休的人，因为他们对退休生活有切身的体会。” 我通常还会说明研究的赞助方或我的学术单位，以进一步证明研究的合法性。

When I can, I begin the interview where the respondent seems already to be. In a study of retirement, if a respondent mentioned, before I turned on the tape recorder, “I’m not actually retired; I’ve got a couple more weeks to go on the job,” I might ask, after starting the tape recorder, “What’s it like, being two weeks before the end of the job? Is that something you think about?” I might then go on to ask how the issue of retirement had arisen while the respondent was on the job, how other people had indicated that they were aware that the respondent was leaving, and how the respondent’s job had changed since he scheduled a retirement date. If there is no evident place to start, I might begin by asking how the respondent happened to enter the situation about which I want to learn. “I would like to ask what your experience has been in retirement, maybe starting with how you happened to retire when you did.”

如果条件允许，我会从受访者似乎已经准备好的话题切入访谈。例如，在一项关于退休的研究中，如果受访者在我打开录音机之前提到“我其实还没退休，还有几周才下班”，那么在开始录音后，我可能会问：“离退休还有两周，感觉如何？你会考虑这个问题吗？” 接着，我可能会进一步询问受访者在职期间是如何萌生退休念头的，其他人是如何表示他们知道受访者即将离职的，以及受访者自确定退休日期以来，工作发生了哪些变化。如果没有明显的切入点，我可能会先问问受访者是如何进入我想要了解的这个情境的。“我想了解一下您的退休经历，或许可以从您当初是如何选择在那个时间退休开始说起。”

In a pilot study of people who are HIV positive I generally started with how it happened that respondents got tested rather than how it happened that they became HIV positive, since their experience as people who were HIV positive actually began with the testing, not with the infection. Here is the start of my interview with one HIV-positive respondent:

在一项针对艾滋病毒感染者的试点研究中，我通常先询问受访者是如何接受检测的，而不是他们是如何感染艾滋病毒的，因为他们作为艾滋病毒感染者的经历实际上是从检测开始的，而不是从感染开始的。以下是我对一位艾滋病毒感染者的访谈开篇：

And so we start. The phrase, “Could you just walk me through …” suggests the level of detail I would like the respondent to provide.

那么，我们就开始吧。“您能给我简单介绍一下……”这句话表明了我希望受访者提供的细节程度。

In this excerpt I made explicit the terms of the interviewing relationship. After introducing the study and myself, I said, “What I’m doing is talking to people who are in your situation, because you know what is going on and nobody else does…. So I’m going to ask you to work with me to tell your story.” Often, I don’t describe in such detail the interviewing relationship I hope to establish, because it seems to me already pretty much understood. In this case the respondent must have struck me as uncertain of what would be expected of him.

在这段摘录中，我明确阐述了访谈关系的条款。在介绍完研究内容和我自己之后，我说：“我正在与和你处境相同的人交谈，因为你知道发生了什么，而其他人却不知道……所以我希望你能配合我，讲述你的故事。” 通常情况下，我不会如此详细地描述我希望建立的访谈关系，因为我觉得这种关系已经基本明了。但在这个案例中，受访者给我的感觉一定是不确定自己应该做什么。

THE INTERVIEWING RELATIONSHIP

# ↩

面试关系

The interviewing relationship is a research partnership between the interviewer and the respondent. The terms of this research partnership are ordinarily implicit, but if I were drafting a contract between myself and a respondent, I would include the following clauses:

访谈关系是访谈者和受访者之间的一种研究伙伴关系。这种研究伙伴关系的条款通常是隐含的，但如果我要起草一份我和受访者之间的合同，我会加入以下条款：

  1. The interviewer and the respondent will work together to produce information useful to the research project.
    访谈者和受访者将共同努力，获取对研究项目有用的信息。
  2. The interviewer will define the areas for exploration and will monitor the quality of the material. The respondent will provide observations, external and internal, accepting the interviewer’s guidance regarding topics and the kind of report that is needed.
    访谈者将界定访谈范围，并监控访谈材料的质量。受访者将提供外部和内部观察结果，并接受访谈者关于访谈主题和所需报告类型的指导。
  3. The interviewer will not ask questions out of idle curiosity. On the other hand, the interviewer will be a privileged inquirer in the sense that the interviewer may ask for information the respondent would not make generally available, maybe would not tell anyone else at all.
    面试官不会出于无谓的好奇心而提问。另一方面，面试官会采取特权提问的方式，可能会询问受访者通常不会公开的信息，甚至可能根本不会告诉任何人。
  4. The interviewer will respect the respondent’s integrity. This means that the interviewer will not question the respondent’s appraisals, choices, motives, right to observations, or personal worth.
    面试官将尊重受访者的诚信。这意味着面试官不会质疑受访者的评价、选择、动机、观察权或个人价值。
  5. The interviewer will ensure, both during the interview and afterward, that the respondent will not be damaged or disadvantaged because of the respondent’s participation in the interview. In particular, the interviewer will treat the respondent’s participation and communications as confidential information.
    访谈员将在访谈过程中及访谈结束后确保受访者不会因参与访谈而受到任何损害或不利影响。尤其需要注意的是，访谈员将对受访者的参与和交流内容严格保密。

There are other ways, besides the research partnership, of defining the interviewing relationship. Sometimes interviewers present themselves as the means by which the respondent can tell his story: “Through me you can make your story known.” This might be the approach of someone doing life history studies or of a reporter in an interview with the famous or the notorious.

除了研究伙伴关系之外，还有其他方式可以定义访谈关系。有时，访谈者会把自己定位为受访者讲述故事的媒介：“通过我，你可以讲述你的故事。” 这可能是进行人生历程研究的人，或是记者采访名人或恶名昭彰者时所采用的方法。

It is also possible for the interviewer to take the role of the respectful student, awaiting instruction. One woman, an excellent interviewer, said she tried to make the government officials she interviewed feel that she was ready to admire their knowledge and authority and was, indeed, already awed to be in the presence of someone so important. She believed that disguising how much she knew and how perceptive and skeptical she was disarmed her respondents.

面试官也可以扮演恭敬的学生角色，等待指导。一位优秀的面试官说，她努力让受访的政府官员感受到，她愿意欣赏他们的学识和权威，并且确实对能与如此重要的人物相处感到敬畏。她认为，掩饰自己的渊博知识、敏锐洞察力和怀疑精神，能够消除受访者的戒备。

Some interviewers are willing to act as the respondentsߣ antagonists. If they suspect the respondent is holding back information, they are ready to confront the respondent: “You say you haven’t ever used drugs. But you hung out with drug users. There must have been a time when you experimented.” Interviews in police stations, of course, take on this quality, as do some employment interviews. Journalists sometimes read up on respondents, the better to confound the respondentsߣ efforts to dissemble.

有些采访者乐于扮演受访者的对立面。如果他们怀疑受访者有所隐瞒，就会毫不犹豫地质问：“你说你从没吸过毒，但你和吸毒者混在一起，肯定有过尝试的时候。” 当然，警局的采访以及一些求职面试也带有这种色彩。记者有时会事先了解受访者的情况，以便更好地揭穿他们的谎言。

In my experience the research partnership definition of the interviewing relationship works best. It is the most easily sustainable, both for the interviewer and the respondent. And it is consistent with the reasons for having research interviews.

根据我的经验，研究伙伴关系对访谈关系的定义最为有效。这种定义最容易维持，对访谈者和受访者而言皆是如此。而且，它也符合开展研究访谈的目的。

SOME INTERVIEWING GUIDELINES

一些面试指导原则

Being a good interviewer requires knowing what kind of information the study needs and being able to help the respondent provide it. Here are some guidelines.

优秀的访谈员需要了解研究需要哪些信息，并能够帮助受访者提供这些信息。以下是一些指导原则。

WHAT IS IT YOU WANT TO OBTAIN IN THE INTERVIEW?

你想通过面试获得什么？

In the great majority of research interviews you will want the respondent to provide concrete descriptions of something he or she has witnessed. This includes both scenes and events external to the respondent and the respondent’s own thoughts and feelings. A task in almost every interview is to communicate to respondents that this is what is needed. Here is an interview excerpt that suggests the kind of information that is wanted and how it can be obtained. It is from an interview with a divorced father who was involved in a dispute with his former wife over his times of visitation. I conducted the interview as part of a study of the usefulness of a program for helping parents deal with visitation problems.

在绝大多数研究访谈中，您都需要受访者提供其亲身经历的具体描述。这包括受访者所处的外部场景和事件，以及受访者自身的想法和感受。几乎每次访谈的一项重要任务是向受访者传达访谈的目的。以下访谈摘录展示了所需信息的类型以及如何获取这些信息。这段摘录来自对一位离异父亲的访谈，他与前妻就探视时间存在争议。我进行此次访谈是为了研究一项旨在帮助父母处理探视问题的项目的有效性。

TRANSCRIPT EXCERPT

文字稿摘录

COMMENTS

评论

R ESPONDENT : It really appalls me that they [in the court] think that I’m some … some, I’m some symbol of money. That is the only reason that I even go to court and the court has any use for me is because I am a symbol of money. That is the only reason. They don’t … they could care less if I saw my son. Okay? It’s a different story if the mother wasn’t seeing him. But they could care less if I didn’t see him. They could care less if I didn’t have a roof over my head. They could care less that I wouldn’t be able to take my son because I don’t have any money to feed him when I have him because I pay all the money out. They don’t care about that.

答辩人：他们（法庭上的那些人）竟然认为我……认为我是个金钱的象征，这真的让我感到震惊。我之所以上法庭，法庭之所以会需要我，仅仅是因为我是个金钱的象征。仅此而已。他们根本……他们根本不在乎我是否能见到我的儿子。明白吗？如果孩子的母亲见不到他，那情况就不同了。但他们根本不在乎我是否能见到他。他们根本不在乎我是否无家可归。他们根本不在乎我是否能带儿子出去，因为我没钱养活他，因为我把所有的钱都花光了。他们根本不在乎这些。

This response, a description of the courts as the respondent views them, is generalized. That it is so emotional may obscure the fact that it summarizes the respondent’s experience rather than presents any specific experience. Note the respondent’s use of “they” when he insists that “they” don’t care about his relationship with his son, only about obtaining money from him for his wife. Later, when the respondent describes a specific incident, he will talk about specific people.

这份答复是对答辩人眼中法院的描述，内容较为笼统。其情绪化的表达可能掩盖了这样一个事实：它概括的是答辩人的经历，而非具体事例。请注意答辩人在强调“他们”不在乎他与儿子的关系，只关心如何从他那里榨取钱财供养妻子时，使用了“他们”一词。之后，当答辩人描述某个具体事件时，他会提及具体的人。

I NTERVIEWER : Could you walk me through the last time you went to court, just what happened?

采访者：您能跟我说说您上次上法庭的情形吗？当时到底发生了什么？

This is a way of asking for the concrete incident that led to the generalized emotional statement. The phrase “walk me through” is intended to communicate the level of concreteness wanted. “The last time” is intended to specify a particular incident.

这是一种询问导致这种笼统情绪表达的具体事件的方式。“请详细描述一下”旨在强调需要具体到什么程度。“上次”则意在指明某个特定事件。

R: The last time I went to court was just before I went to see the counselor. Basically, I went down to go over custody and payments. Now think about it. I got to pay rent. I live in an apartment. I got to pay rent. I got to put food on the table, you know, I got to make payments on the car. I make three hundred dollars a week, gross. Take out my taxes, I make two hundred and forty-seven dollars.

R：我上次去法院就是在见咨询师之前。基本上，我去法院是为了讨论监护权和抚养费的问题。你想想，我得付房租。我住在公寓里。我得付房租。我得养家糊口，你知道，我得还车贷。我每周税前收入三百美元。扣除税款后，我实际到手两百四十七美元。

The respondent provides a time reference for his last time in court and a reason for having gone there but then returns to his outrage.

答辩人提供了他上次出庭的时间和原因，但随后又表达了他的愤怒。

TRANSCRIPT EXCERPT

文字稿摘录

COMMENTS

评论

They want seventy dollars. Who pays for my rent?

他们要价七十美元。谁来付我的房租？

I: Okay. When you came to court, were you waiting around before you …

我：好的。你来法院的时候，是不是一直在外面等着……

I bring the respondent back to the court appearance, to what is likely to have been its beginning—waiting around.

我把被告带回法庭，带回法庭出庭的场景，很可能就是出庭的开始——等待。

R: Oh yeah, wait around for hours, hours.

R：哦，是啊，要等好几个小时，好几个小时。

I: Where were you waiting?

我：你在哪里等的？

I ask for specifics to keep the respondent in the incident.

我要求提供具体细节，以便让受访者了解事件经过。

R: You wait downstairs in a lobby, waiting to be called. And then you go through this shenanigans.

R：你得在楼下的大厅里等着被叫。然后你还得经历这些乱七八糟的事。

I: What happens while you’re waiting to be called?

问：在等待被叫到电话的时候会发生什么？

I’m asking for the concrete details of the incident. Notice that I ask about what happens in the present tense. This is an error, because it encourages a generalized response. (I say more about this later in this chapter.)

我要求提供事件的具体细节。请注意，我用现在时询问发生了什么。这是个错误，因为它容易导致泛泛而谈。（我会在本章后面详细讨论这一点。）

R: You sit. You sit. You sit. You don’t even get called. I had the lawyer go stand in line. You don’t even see a judge. You see some person who shuffles a million people around a day. And then you sit down with a mediator. He’s my mediator. He’s not my mediator. He’s telling me what I’m supposed to do like he’s a judge. He’s telling me, “This is what you have to do.”

This excerpt began with a generalized statement of the court experience of a noncustodial father. I wanted the respondent to move from this to as close to an observer’s report as he could provide of his experiences, internal as well as external. Only that sort of concrete description of just what happened could constitute interpretable data regarding the experiences of noncustodial fathers in court.

这段摘录以一位非监护父亲的法庭经历的概括性陈述开头。我希望答辩人能在此基础上，尽可能以观察者的身份，详细描述他自身的经历，包括内部和外部的感受。只有这种对事件经过的具体描述，才能构成关于非监护父亲在法庭上经历的可解释数据。

Generalized descriptions can be good enough if they are about an issue of peripheral importance to the study. A respondent’s statement that “I go to work about nine in the morning” would be acceptable if the study isn’t especially concerned about the respondentsߣ use of time. But if respondentsߣ use of time is important to the study, the interviewer should attempt to obtain a concrete description of what happened the morning of the day preceding the interview.

如果问题与研究关系不大，那么概括性的描述就足够了。例如，如果研究并非特别关注受访者的时间利用情况，那么受访者“我早上九点左右去上班”这样的陈述是可以接受的。但如果受访者的时间利用情况对研究至关重要，那么访谈员就应该尝试获取受访者在访谈前一天上午的具体情况描述。

We obtain descriptions of specific incidents by asking respondents to particularize. In the foregoing excerpt I asked, “Could you walk me through the last time you went to court, just what happened?” Other questions that might also have served to elicit a concrete description include: “Could you tell me about a time that displays that at its clearest?”; “Is there a specific incident you can think of that would make clear what you have in mind?”; and “Could you tell me what happened, starting from the beginning?”

我们通过要求受访者详细描述事件来获取具体情况。在前面的摘录中，我问道：“您能详细描述一下您上次出庭的情况吗？当时发生了什么？”其他一些可能有助于获得具体描述的问题包括：“您能告诉我一次最能体现这种情况的经历吗？”；“您能想到一个具体的事件来清楚地说明您的想法吗？”；以及“您能从头开始告诉我发生了什么吗？”

It can sometimes seem to an interviewer to be an untrustworthy sampling of respondent behavior to ask only about the last time an incident occurred. To check this, it might be useful for the interviewer to ask if that occurrence was very different from previous occurrences and, if it was, to ask for the occurrence that preceded the most recent one as well. Often, however, the discussion of the most recent occurrence will produce so much instructive particularity that it will be of secondary importance whether it is a typical event or not.

有时，访谈者可能会觉得，只询问受访者最近一次发生事件的情况，不足以全面反映其行为。为了验证这一点，访谈者可以询问该事件是否与以往的事件有很大不同；如果确实不同，则最好也询问最近一次事件之前的事件。然而，通常情况下，对最近一次事件的讨论会揭示出许多极具启发性的细节，以至于该事件是否具有典型性就显得不那么重要了。

TENSE AND SPECIFICITY IN THE INTERVIEW

访谈中的时态和具体性

It is useful to bear in mind that reports of actual events are ordinarily made in the past tense: “I did …,” “He said …,” and so on. However, respondents may also make reports of actual events in the present tense to give their accounts a sense of immediacy and drama, as though the events were happening now. The respondent just quoted did that when he said, “My lawyer’s like, he says, ‘Well, why can’t we have the three weeks?’”

值得注意的是，对实际事件的描述通常使用过去时态，例如“我做了……”，“他说……”等等。然而，为了使叙述更具即时性和戏剧性，仿佛事件正在发生，受访者也可能使用现在时态来描述实际事件。刚才引用的受访者就使用了这种表达方式，他说：“我的律师说，‘为什么我们不能有三周时间？’”

A more frequent use of the present tense might be called “the generalized present.” This is the tense respondents most frequently employ for a generalized description. It summarizes developments that occurred in the past and continue through the present. This is the tense used by the respondent in the excerpt just presented when he said, “You sit. You sit. You sit. You don’t even get called.” Notice that the respondent used the generalized present in response to a question by the interviewer that was itself in the generalized present: “What happens while you’re waiting to be called?” This question assumed the generalized present and so pulled a response in the generalized present. A better question would have been, “What happened while you were waiting to be called?”

现在时的一种更常见的用法可以称为“概括性现在时”。这是受访者最常用于概括性描述的时态。它概括了过去发生并延续到现在的事件。例如，在刚才的摘录中，受访者就使用了这种时态，他说：“你坐着。你坐着。你坐着。你甚至都没人叫你。” 请注意，受访者使用概括性现在时来回答面试官提出的一个问题，而这个问题本身也是用概括性现在时提出的：“在你等待被叫到的时候发生了什么？” 这个问题假定了概括性现在时，因此得到的回答也是概括性现在时。一个更好的问题应该是：“在你等待被叫到的时候发生了什么？”

The generalized present is often requested in studies using a fixedquestion—open-response format. Such a study might ask, for example, “What are the issues about which you and your wife tend to disagree?” As was exemplified in the excerpt, when a question is phrased in the generalized present, the response is likely to be in the generalized present.

在采用固定问题-开放式回答形式的研究中，通常会要求受访者使用一般现在时。例如，这类研究可能会问：“你和你妻子在哪些问题上容易产生分歧？” 正如摘录中的例子所示，当问题以一般现在时表述时，受访者的回答也可能使用一般现在时。

There is a second generalizing tense, which I call “the generalized past.” A respondent can signal this by use of the auxiliary “would,” as in “I would sit there for hours.” The respondent could also signal this tense by using “used to” or an equivalent: “I used to spend a whole day sitting there.” Here too the respondent is summarizing, not describing a specific incident. 1

还有第二种概括性时态，我称之为“概括性过去时”。受访者可以使用助动词“would”来表示这种时态，例如“我会坐在那里几个小时”。受访者也可以使用“used to”或类似词语来表示这种时态：“我过去常常在那里坐一整天。”这里，受访者同样是在进行概括，而不是描述某个具体事件。

Respondents often prefer to provide generalized accounts rather than concrete instances, One reason for this is that they can feel that they are being more responsible reporters if they remain general, since they are describing an entire class of events rather than a single idiosyncratic event. The generalized material, they may think, is more inclusive and so constitutes better information. Actually, when respondents provide generalized accounts, their description expresses a kind of theory of what is most typical or most nearly essential in the class of the event. By doing this, respondents preempt the investigator’s task of analysis; it is they who have decided what is important. 2

受访者通常更倾向于提供概括性的描述而非具体事例。原因之一是，他们认为保持概括性描述能让他们感觉自己更有责任感，因为他们描述的是一类事件，而非单一的个别事件。他们可能认为，概括性的内容更具包容性，因此能提供更好的信息。实际上，当受访者提供概括性描述时，他们的描述表达了一种关于该类事件中最典型或最接近本质特征的理论。通过这种方式，受访者抢占了调查者的分析工作；是他们决定了什么是重要的。

In addition, a generalized account permits respondents to minimize elements about which they feel diffident. Respondents may feel that generalized accounts are appropriate for a report to someone like the interviewer, whom they don’t know that well. Generalized accounts are more nearly public information, with none of the potentially embarrassing or revealing details of private life.

此外，概括性的描述允许受访者尽量减少他们不愿提及的内容。受访者可能认为，对于像访谈者这样不太熟悉的人，概括性的描述更为合适。概括性的描述更接近于公开信息，不包含任何可能令人尴尬或泄露隐私的私人生活细节。

Interviewers, in qualitative interview studies, like their respondents, may imagine that the generalized present or generalized past will provide an overview that saves interview time and is less subject to the idiosyncrasies of the specific event. In addition, the interviewers may unconsciously prefer to phrase a question in the generalized present or past because it seems less prying, less intrusive, than a question that asks for a specific past event. The question, “What’s it like when you and your wife quarrel?” can feel easier to ask than “Can you tell me about your most recent quarrel? Could you walk me through it?” Asking about a specific past event can make interviewers uncomfortable because it seems as though they are putting respondents on the spot.

在定性访谈研究中，访谈者可能和受访者一样，认为概括性的现在或过去情况能够提供一个概览，既节省访谈时间，又能减少具体事件的特殊性。此外，访谈者可能无意识地倾向于用概括性的现在或过去情况来提问，因为这似乎比询问具体过去事件的问题更不具侵入性、更不冒犯。例如，“你和妻子吵架时是什么感觉？”这个问题可能比“你能跟我说说你最近一次吵架的情况吗？你能详细描述一下吗？”更容易开口。询问具体过去事件会让访谈者感到不自在，因为这似乎会让受访者感到尴尬。

But just because questions phrased in the generalized present or generalized past appear less intrusive, the interviewer should be wary of them. The point of qualitative interviewing is to obtain from respondents a field report on their external and internal experiences. This does require the respondent to provide a density of detail that would not be provided in ordinary conversation. If asking for detailed, concrete information in an interview constitutes an unacceptable invasion of privacy, the interviewing partnership is faulty.

但即便使用概括性的现在时或过去时提出的问题看似不那么具有侵入性，访谈者也应保持警惕。定性访谈的目的是从受访者那里获得关于其外部和内部体验的实地报告。这确实要求受访者提供在日常对话中不会涉及的丰富细节。如果在访谈中询问详细、具体的信息构成不可接受的隐私侵犯，那么访谈关系就存在问题。

QUESTIONS TO ASK

要问的问题

There are no magic questions. Any question is a good question if it directs the respondent to material needed by the study in a way that makes it easy for the respondent to provide the material. Sometimes the best question is one that in a very few words directs the respondent to give more detail or fill in a gap: “What happened then?” Sometimes it is one that takes the time to tell the respondent just what is now needed: “Could you give me a concrete instance of that, a time that actually happened, with as much detail as you can?” Any question that helps the respondent produce the material you need is a good question.

没有所谓的“魔法问题”。只要问题能引导受访者提供研究所需的信息，并且便于受访者提供，那么它就是好问题。有时，最好的问题可以用寥寥数语引导受访者提供更多细节或填补信息空白，例如：“后来发生了什么？”有时，最好的问题则需要花时间直接告诉受访者现在需要什么：“您能否举一个具体的例子，一个实际发生过的事情，并尽可能详细地描述？”任何有助于受访者提供所需信息的问题都是好问题。

On Phrasing the Question

关于问题的措辞

Should every question be phrased in an open way, or might a question be a leading one in that it anticipates a response? Do you ask “What were your feelings then?” or “Were you unhappy about that?” Or might you even offer “You must have been unhappy”?

每个问题都应该以开放式的方式提出吗？还是说有些问题带有引导性，预设了某种回答？你是问“你当时是什么感受？”或者“你为此感到不高兴吗？”，甚至直接说“你当时一定很不高兴吧？”

Most often, you will not want to affect the respondent’s report by offering anticipations in your questions. If you have no reason to anticipate a particular response, you would ask, “What were your feelings when that was happening?” But sometimes you can help a respondent provide a full report by demonstrating your understanding, and one way to do this is to name the respondent’s state. In this situation the right thing to say might be “You must have been unhappy about that.” Or if you don’t want to supply the characterization, “unhappy”—after all, if you do, the characterization of the feeling isn’t the respondent’s own—you might try “It sounds as though you had a pretty strong reaction.” You don’t have to be compulsively nondirective, but you should make sure that the words and images you may eventually quote in your report are the respondent’s, not yours.

大多数情况下，你不希望在提问中预设受访者的回答，从而影响他们的陈述。如果你没有理由预设某种特定的回答，你可以问：“当时你是什么感受？” 但有时，你可以通过展现你的理解来帮助受访者提供完整的陈述，而一种方法就是描述受访者当时的感受。在这种情况下，恰当的说法可能是：“你当时一定很不高兴。” 如果你不想直接用“不高兴”来描述——毕竟，如果你用了，这种描述就不是受访者自己的感受——你可以尝试说：“听起来你的反应相当强烈。” 你不必刻意避免引导，但你应该确保最终在报告中引用的词语和描述都来自受访者，而不是你自己的。

There may be a few points in an interview where you want to check on a surmise you have come to. One way to do this is to say, “It sounds like you are still pretty upset about that.” But if the respondent agrees with this, you might do well to check whether the agreement comes because of politeness or because you have been right. I have sometimes asked “Is that exactly right?” just to make sure.

在访谈过程中，你可能偶尔会想确认一下自己的推测。一种方法是说：“听起来你对这件事仍然很耿耿于怀。”但如果受访者表示同意，你最好弄清楚他们的同意是出于礼貌还是因为你的推测是正确的。为了确保万无一失，我有时会问：“是这样吗？”

Helping Respondents Develop Information

帮助受访者提供信息

Most important in an interview is obtaining concrete information in the area of inquiry. Once a respondent has alluded to an actual incident, perhaps in response to your asking, with respect to something of importance to the study, “Could you tell me the most recent time that happened?”, you may have to help the respondent develop the incident adequately. Here are forms of development you might want to obtain and some ways you might ask for them.

访谈中最重要的是获取与研究主题相关的具体信息。一旦受访者提及某个实际事件（例如，在您询问与研究相关的某个重要问题时，例如“您能告诉我最近一次发生这件事是什么时候吗？”），您可能需要帮助受访者充分展开叙述。以下是一些您可能需要了解的信息类型以及一些提问方式。

  1. Extending . You might want to know what led to an incident. Questions that ask for this include “How did that start?” “What led to that?” Or you might want to know the consequences of an incident: “Could you go on with that? What happened next?”
    进一步询问。你可能想知道事件的起因。这类问题包括“事情是怎么开始的？”“是什么导致了这件事？”或者你可能想知道事件的后果：“你能继续做下去吗？接下来发生了什么？”
  2. Filling in detail . You might want more detail than the respondent has provided. A useful question often is “Could you walk me through it?” An interviewer who worked with me used to add “We need you to be as detailed as possible,” and that seemed to work for her. Another approach to obtaining increased detail is to go to the beginning of the respondent’s story for which you want detail and ask what followed, exemplifying in your question the density of detail you want: “So you were sitting there, talking with your guest, and this other fellow came over. What happened then?” You could even add “Can you walk me through it?”
    补充细节。你可能需要比受访者提供的更多细节。一个常用的问法是“你能跟我详细说说吗？”。我以前的一位面试官会补充说“我们需要你尽可能详细地描述”，这似乎对她很有效。另一种获取更多细节的方法是，从受访者讲述你想了解的细节开始，询问接下来发生了什么，并在问题中体现你想要的细节程度：“所以你当时坐在那里，和你的客人聊天，然后另一个人走了过来。之后发生了什么？”你甚至可以加上一句“你能跟我详细说说吗？”
  3. Identifying actors . You might want to learn the social context of an incident, the other people who were there. You could ask “Was anyone else there when that was happening?” “Who else was there and what did they do?”
    识别事件参与者。你可能需要了解事件的社会背景，以及当时在场的其他人员。你可以问：“事发时还有其他人在场吗？”“还有谁在场？他们做了什么？”
  4. Others the respondent consulted . Especially in a study whose concerns include how respondents dealt with problems, you may want to ask whom the respondent talked with about an incident and what the respondent said: “Did you talk to anyone about what was going on?” This may also produce information about the respondent’s view of the incident at the time.
    受访者咨询过的其他人。尤其是在一项关注受访者如何处理问题的研究中，你可能需要询问受访者就某件事与谁交谈过，以及受访者说了些什么：“你有没有和别人谈过这件事？” 这也有助于了解受访者当时对事件的看法。
  5. Inner events . You will generally want to obtain information regarding some of the inner events that accompanied the outer events the respondent reports. Inner events include perceptions, what the respondent heard or saw; cognitions, what the respondent thought, believed, or decided; and emotions, how the respondent felt and what strivings and impulses the respondent experienced. They can also include the respondent’s preconceptions, values, goals, hopes, and fears. You will usually want at least the cognitive and emotional events. Imagine a respondent reporting, “My boss called me in and told me he wanted me to fire one of the people working for me.” After the respondent developed what happened, you could ask the respondent to describe his or her cognitive reactions by asking, “When that was happening, what thoughts did you have?” Then you might obtain emotional reactions by asking, “What were your feelings when he said that?” or “Can you remember how you reacted, emotionally?”
    内在事件。您通常需要了解受访者报告的外部事件背后伴随的一些内在事件。内在事件包括感知（受访者听到或看到的内容）、认知（受访者的想法、信念或决定）以及情绪（受访者的感受、努力和冲动）。它们还可以包括受访者的先入之见、价值观、目标、希望和恐惧。您通常至少需要了解认知和情绪事件。例如，假设一位受访者报告说：“我的老板把我叫去，告诉我他要我解雇我的一名下属。”在受访者描述完事情经过后，您可以询问受访者描述其认知反应，例如：“当时你有什么想法？”然后，您可以通过询问“他说那句话时你的感受是什么？”或“你还记得你的情绪反应吗？”来了解其情绪反应。
  6. Making indications explicit . Respondents may indicate by a gesture, a grimace, or an expressive shrug feelings they haven’t put into words. You won’t have the gesture, grimace, or shrug in your transcript when you are analyzing your data, nor can you quote it as supporting material for your report. The problem is to communicate to the respondent that you sort of understand what he or she is indicating but that you want to be sure. To convey the message that the respondent’s feelings are worth developing in words, you might try suggesting, perhaps by a nod, that you understand, and then ask for elaboration by the question, “You had some pretty definite feelings?” or “What were the feelings you had?”
    明确表达。受访者可能会通过手势、表情或耸肩来表达他们未曾用语言表达的感受。在分析数据时，你无法在访谈记录中看到这些手势、表情或耸肩，也无法将其作为报告的佐证材料引用。问题在于如何让受访者明白你大致理解了他们的意图，但你想确认一下。为了传达受访者的感受值得用语言表达的信息，你可以尝试点头表示理解，然后询问“你当时有一些非常明确的感受吗？”或“你当时的感受是什么？”

Handling Difficult Questions

处理棘手问题

Some questions are hard to ask. People in survey research sometimes say that income is the most private of matters, more difficult to ask about than sexual behavior. Perhaps, but sexual behavior is difficult enough. However, often there is a relatively tactful way of entering a difficult area. To learn about men’s extramarital experiences, in the study of how occupationally successful men organized their lives, we sometimes began by asking respondents about their experience of loneliness and then moved to questions about friendships with women other than their wives. Still, despite our efforts to be as tactful as possible, a few men responded by saying that they didn’t want to get into that area. That told us something—although not very much.

有些问题难以启齿。调查研究人员有时会说，收入是最私密的话题，比性行为更难问。或许如此，但性行为本身也足够棘手了。然而，通常还是有一些相对委婉的方式来切入敏感领域。为了了解男性的婚外情经历，在研究事业成功的男性如何安排生活时，我们有时会先询问受访者的孤独感，然后再探讨他们与妻子以外的女性的友谊。尽管我们尽力做到委婉，但仍有一些男性表示他们不想涉足这个领域。这告诉我们一些信息——虽然信息量不大。

In general, if there are difficult issues to be developed, it is important to establish a reliable research relationship before entering the area. It is also important for interviewers to know why the information is needed. Interviewers in any study should always understand its goals, so that they can know which of a respondent’s leads to develop; but if they are to ask about sensitive issues, it is especially important that they know why they are asking. And they must thoroughly believe in the study’s right to know. Otherwise they will communicate their absence of confidence in the questions.

一般来说，如果需要深入探讨一些棘手的问题，那么在进入该领域之前建立可靠的研究关系至关重要。此外，访谈员必须清楚了解收集信息的目的。任何研究的访谈员都应始终理解研究目标，以便知道应该跟进受访者提供的哪些线索；但如果需要询问敏感问题，他们就更应该清楚自己提问的原因。而且，他们必须坚信研究有权获取这些信息。否则，他们的提问会显得缺乏自信。

Markers

标记

I define a marker as a passing reference made by a respondent to an important event or feeling state. One respondent whom I interviewed in the study of retirement reported, “We went to our place on the Cape a couple of weeks after my mother died, and my husband spent all his time working on the house. He always has one more thing he has to do.” The point of this response was to communicate how occupied the respondent’s husband was, despite his retirement. The reference to the death of the respondent’s mother—not previously mentioned by her—was a marker. The respondent was indicating that this was something significant for her, by which she dated events; that she understood that it might not be important for the study; and that if I wanted to pick it up, well, there it was.

我将“标记”定义为受访者对重要事件或情感状态的简要提及。在我进行的一项关于退休的研究中，一位受访者说道：“我母亲去世几周后，我们去了我们在科德角的房子，我丈夫把所有时间都花在了修缮房子上。他总是觉得还有一件事要做。” 这段话的重点在于表明，尽管已经退休，她的丈夫仍然非常忙碌。她提到母亲去世——此前她从未提及——这便是一个标记。受访者表明，这件事对她来说意义重大，她以此来判断事件发生的先后顺序；她也明白这件事可能对研究本身并不重要；而且，如果我需要深入探讨，她也知道这件事就在那里。

After the respondent had finished developing the material about her husband’s full schedule, I said, “You mentioned earlier that your mother had died. What happened?” The respondent then described how devoted she had been to her mother. That devotion explained why her inaccessibility to her husband had been an issue in his retirement. Now, with her mother dead, there were indications that things might be different. This was material important to the study.

在受访者讲述完她丈夫繁忙的日程安排后，我问道：“您之前提到过您的母亲去世了。发生了什么事？” 受访者随后描述了她对母亲的孝顺。正是这份孝顺解释了为什么在她丈夫退休后，她难以与他相处。如今，母亲去世，种种迹象表明情况可能会有所不同。这些信息对本研究至关重要。

Because markers occur in the course of talking about something else, you may have to remember them and then return to them when you can, saying, “A few minutes ago you mentioned …” But it is a good idea to pick up a marker as soon as you conveniently can if the material it hints at could in any way be relevant for your study. Letting the marker go will demonstrate to the respondent that the area is not of importance for you. It can also demonstrate that you are only interested in answers to your questions, not in the respondent’s full experience.

由于线索往往出现在谈论其他事情的过程中，你可能需要记住它们，并在合适的时机再次提及，例如说：“几分钟前您提到过……”。但如果线索所暗示的内容可能与你的研究有任何关联，最好尽快抓住它。如果忽略线索，会让受访者觉得你并不重视这个领域。这也会让他们觉得你只关心问题的答案，而对受访者的完整经历不感兴趣。

Sometimes interviewers feel it is tactful not to pick up markers. This may, on occasion, be true, especially if the marker was dropped inadvertently. But most often respondents are in enough control of their report that if they don’t want you to know about the area, they won’t drop markers.

有时，面试官会觉得不捡起标记物是一种礼貌的做法。这种情况偶尔确实存在，尤其是在标记物是无意中掉落的情况下。但大多数情况下，受访者对自己的回答有足够的掌控力，如果他们不想让你知道相关区域的情况，他们就不会故意掉落标记物。

Respondents sometimes offer markers by indicating that much has happened that they aren’t talking about. They might say, for example, “Well, there was a lot going on at that time.” It is then reasonable to respond, “Could you tell me about that?” It is different when a respondent clearly states that an area is off-limits to the interview by saying something like, “There was a lot going on at that time, but I don’t want to talk about that.” Now you can’t possibly ask, “Could you tell me about that?” Still, if the topic appears relevant to the study and you have a good interviewing relationship, you might ask, “Can you tell me anything about what sort of thing that was?”

受访者有时会通过暗示他们有很多事情不想谈及来提供线索。例如，他们可能会说：“嗯，当时发生了很多事。”这时，你可以合理地回应：“您能跟我说说吗？”但如果受访者明确表示某个话题不在访谈范围内，比如说道：“当时发生了很多事，但我不想谈这个。”那就另当别论了。这时你就不能再问“您能跟我说说吗？”了。不过，如果这个话题与研究相关，而且你和受访者关系良好，你或许可以问：“您能跟我说说那件事具体是什么样的吗？”

MANAGING THE INTERVIEW

面试技巧

Intrusions

入侵

The first rule of interviewing is that if the respondent has something to say, the respondent must be able to say it. If you find yourself talking over the respondent, interrupting, or holding the floor while the respondent tries to interrupt, something is going wrong in the interview. You might want to withdraw some of your attention from the respondent for a moment or two to figure out why you are competing for the floor. But whether you figure it out or not, you ought to stop doing it.

访谈的第一条原则是：如果受访者有话要说，就必须能够表达出来。如果你发现自己一直在打断受访者、抢话，或者在受访者试图插话时仍然占据主导地位，那么访谈就出了问题。你或许应该暂时把注意力从受访者身上移开一两分钟，思考一下自己为什么会和受访者争夺话语权。但无论你是否找到了原因，都应该立即停止这种行为。

It is easy to intrude in an interview. You can interrupt the respondent. You can finish the respondent’s sentences. You can offer your associations to what the respondent is saying. You can suggest explanations for observations about which the respondent is perplexed; for example, if the respondent shrugs and says, “I don’t know why he said that,” you could propose, “Well, maybe he was trying to defend himself.” You can insist on completing your question even if the respondent has already started to answer. You can hop from issue to issue following your own train of thought rather than the respondent’s. With any and all of these, don’t do it.

在访谈中，很容易出现插话的情况。你可以打断受访者，替他们把话说完，或者对受访者所说的话妄加评论。你还可以为受访者感到困惑的某些观点提供解释；例如，如果受访者耸耸肩说：“我不知道他为什么这么说”，你可以说：“嗯，也许他是在为自己辩解。”即使受访者已经开始回答，你也可以坚持问完自己的问题。你还可以跳着话题，按照自己的思路而不是受访者的思路，从一个话题跳到另一个话题。对于以上任何一种情况，都不要这样做。

Never, never fight for control of the interview. The interview is a collaboration. If it should happen that a respondent is developing an irrelevant topic at great length, you may have to interrupt to say that there’s another topic you would like to get to. But that should be done in the spirit of the collaboration; it’s your responsibility to set topics. You can usually manage the redirection without discouraging the respondent from talking freely. In the retirement study a respondent who was nearing retirement wanted to talk about the details of his business and how hectic things were. His discussion was interesting but not useful for the study, so at a pause I asked, “With all this going on, is it possible for you also to plan for retirement?” We then moved to discuss the respondent’s planning for his retirement.

永远不要试图控制访谈。访谈是一种合作。如果受访者滔滔不绝地谈论一个无关的话题，你可能需要打断他，说明你想讨论另一个话题。但这应该本着合作的精神进行；设定话题是你的责任。通常情况下，你可以在不打断受访者畅所欲言的情况下，巧妙地引导话题。在退休研究中，一位即将退休的受访者想谈谈他生意上的细节以及工作有多么繁忙。他的谈话很有趣，但对研究本身并无帮助，所以我趁着谈话间隙问道：“在如此繁忙的情况下，您还有时间规划退休吗？” 然后，我们转而讨论了这位受访者的退休规划。

Talking About Yourself

谈论自己

The interview is about the respondent, not about the interviewer. In my view, at least until the interviewing has ended, the interviewer should do only as much self-reporting as is consistent with the interview situation. It is usually enough for the interviewer to give business card information—location and profession—along with the study’s aims and sponsorship.

访谈的重点在于受访者，而非访谈者。在我看来，至少在访谈结束之前，访谈者应该只进行与访谈情境相符的自我介绍。通常情况下，访谈者只需提供名片信息（例如所在地和职业），以及研究目的和赞助方即可。

If a respondent asks about some aspect of the study, the question should be answered fully—although not so fully that the respondent’s attention wanders. If a respondent asks a question of the interviewer such as whether the interviewer had a difficult time finding the respondent’s home, the question should be answered in a way that will satisfy the respondent’s concern, but briefly. If a respondent asks a specific personal question, such as whether the interviewer had an experience similar to the one the respondent is describing, the interviewer should answer honestly rather than seem mysterious. But again the response should be brief; it’s the respondent’s experience that’s important.

如果受访者询问有关研究的某个方面，应完整回答，但不要过于详细，以免分散受访者的注意力。如果受访者询问访谈员一些问题，例如访谈员是否难以找到受访者的住址，则应以简明扼要的方式解答，以消除受访者的疑虑。如果受访者询问具体的个人问题，例如访谈员是否有过与受访者描述类似的经历，访谈员应如实回答，避免故弄玄虚。但同样，回答应简洁明了；重要的是受访者的体验。

Some interviewers believe that self-disclosure fosters disclosure by respondents. I don’t have much experience with self-disclosure as a facilitative technique, but the experience I do have leads me to question it. My own experience is that self-disclosure complicates an interview situation by shifting the respondent’s attention to the interviewer and altering the respondent’s relationship with the interviewer.

有些访谈者认为，自我披露能促进受访者的自我披露。我在这方面的经验不多，但我的经验让我对此持怀疑态度。我的经验是，自我披露会使访谈情况变得复杂，因为它会将受访者的注意力转移到访谈者身上，并改变受访者与访谈者之间的关系。

Monitoring the Information the Respondent Is Providing

监测受访者提供的信息

You must carry into the interview a general idea of what you want to learn about. The interview guide is one statement of this. Your ability to judge what else might contribute to the study’s report should make it possible to recognize when material not anticipated in the guide could be useful for the study. Even as you are listening closely, you should be assessing whether the material might be useful for the study’s report. The guiding question is “Does this material help illuminate experience in the area of the study?”

你必须带着想要了解的内容的大致思路去参加访谈。访谈指南就是这方面的一个说明。你应该能够判断哪些信息可能对研究报告有所贡献，从而识别出指南中未提及但可能对研究有用的材料。即使在认真倾听的同时，你也应该评估这些材料是否对研究报告有用。指导性问题是：“这些材料是否有助于阐明研究领域的相关经验？”

Suppose your study is on the psychological and emotional concomitants of being engaged in a lawsuit. Your concern is what it feels like to be either the person sued or the person doing the suing. In an exploratory interview you find yourself being told by a plaintiff about his experiences as a father when his son got into a dispute over ownership of baseball cards. Is this relevant material? Should you ask for its development in the interview? Or should you be thinking about how to redirect the respondent? If I could imagine any use for the material, I would want the respondent to develop it. It might occur to me that the stance of being a father protecting his child, or teaching the child to deal with conflict, carries over into the respondent’s present adversarial action. For me, that possibility would be enough to justify encouraging the respondent to develop the material.

假设你的研究是关于诉讼过程中伴随而来的心理和情感因素。你关注的是作为被告或原告的感受。在一次探索性访谈中，一位原告讲述了他作为父亲的经历：他的儿子曾因棒球卡的归属权与人发生争执。这是否与研究相关？你是否应该在访谈中要求原告详细阐述？或者，你是否应该考虑如何引导原告继续讲述？如果我认为这段素材有任何用途，我会希望原告继续阐述。我可能会想到，作为父亲保护孩子或教导孩子如何处理冲突的立场，会延续到原告当前的诉讼行为中。对我而言，这种可能性就足以成为鼓励原告继续阐述这段素材的理由。

It can be hard to know what is relevant, especially in early interviews, before the frame of the study is firmly established. My policy is: If in doubt, see what’s there.

尤其是在研究框架尚未完全确立的早期访谈阶段，很难判断哪些信息是相关的。我的做法是：如有疑问，就看看访谈内容。

Adequacy of the Respondent’s Account

答辩人陈述的充分性

Suppose what you are being told is in exactly the right area. How do you know whether you are being told enough, whether you are being given enough development and enough detail? One test is visualizability. Can you call up the scene and imagine who is there in the setting being described and how the participants relate to each other? If you were to stage the scene in a theater, would you know what people to put there? Would you know who is saying what? Would you be able to move the plot forward? Actually, you’ll never get enough information to do all of this, but you ought to be able to identify the major figures present on the scene, know the important things that were said, and maybe understand how the scene came to be or what happened next. If an event is of critical importance for your study, you should try to get as much information about what happened as your respondent can supply, up to the point where the respondent becomes restive.

假设你得到的信息完全正确。你如何判断信息是否足够，是否提供了足够的展开和细节？一个检验方法是视觉化。你能否在脑海中浮现出场景，想象出描述中的人物，以及他们之间的关系？如果要在剧院里重现这个场景，你知道该安排哪些演员吗？你知道谁在说什么吗？你能推动剧情发展吗？实际上，你永远不可能获得足够的信息来完成所有这些，但你应该能够识别出场景中的主要人物，了解重要的对话内容，或许还能理解场景是如何发生的，或者接下来发生了什么。如果某个事件对你的研究至关重要，你应该尽可能多地收集受访者提供的信息，直到他们开始感到不安为止。

Managing Transitions

过渡管理

The best questions fit in so well with what respondents are saying that they seem almost to be continuations of the respondentsߣ own associations. They encourage respondents to say more about what is already in their minds. Transitions to new topics require respondents to stop and think, to relocate themselves; they may be necessary, but they tend to be unsettling.

最好的问题与受访者的回答如此契合，以至于它们几乎像是受访者自身联想的延续。这些问题鼓励受访者进一步表达他们心中已有的想法。话题的转换需要受访者停下来思考，重新调整思路；虽然这种转换或许是必要的，但往往会让人感到不安。

Suppose that after a respondent has told an anecdote about his children, the interviewer nods and then asks, “How about at work, what is a typical day like?” The respondent will require time to reorient himself. He must redirect his mind from his relationship with his kids to his work situation. For a few moments, the respondent is apt to flounder. The verbal expression of this might be, “Well, ah, well, ah, the way it goes, I guess …” The interviewer has flustered the respondent.

假设一位受访者讲述了一个关于孩子的趣事后，面试官点点头，然后问道：“那么在工作中呢？您典型的一天是什么样的？” 受访者需要一些时间来调整思路。他必须将注意力从与孩子的关系转移到工作上。在最初的几分钟里，受访者可能会一时语塞。他可能会这样说：“嗯，啊，嗯，啊，大概就是这样吧……” 面试官让受访者有些不知所措。

I used to tell interviewers who worked for me that they could fluster respondents three times in an interview. Anything more and the respondent would wait for the next question, answer it briefly, and then wait for the next question. This is how respondents act in survey interviews. It isn’t at all what is wanted in qualitative interviews.

我以前常跟我的面试官说，他们可以在一次访谈中让受访者感到不知所措三次。如果超过三次，受访者就会等着下一个问题，简短回答一下，然后再等下一个问题。这是调查访谈中受访者的表现，但完全不是定性访谈所需要的。

Actually, how many times a respondent can be flustered and yet remain ready to give a full report depends largely on the quality of the interviewing partnership. A fully cooperative respondent can be flustered more than the three times I would tell interviewers was their limit. But where there is initial resistance—for example, where a respondent isn’t sure he or she wants to be interviewed—even a single flustering can lead to responses that are stiff and sparse.

事实上，受访者能够经历多少次慌乱却仍能提供完整报告，很大程度上取决于访谈双方的合作质量。一位完全配合的受访者可以经历超过三次慌乱的次数，而我通常认为三次是受访者的极限。但如果受访者一开始就有所抵触——例如，他们不确定自己是否愿意接受采访——即使只有一次慌乱，也可能导致回答生硬且简短。

It is good practice to try to follow the respondent’s associations so long as they remain within the interview’s frame. The interviewer will still have a great deal of influence on the direction the respondent’s associations take. The interviewer will be constantly communicating—by nods of agreement and understanding as well as by questions and comments—what is of value to the study and what is not. Even if few directive questions are asked, the interview will be an interactive product. Usually, without introducing new topics more than three or four times in the interview, the interviewer will find that the issues that have to be covered have been dealt with.

只要受访者的联想不超出访谈范围，顺应他们的联想是一种良好的做法。访谈者仍然会对受访者联想的方向产生很大的影响。访谈者会不断地通过点头表示同意和理解，以及提问和评论，来传达哪些内容对研究有价值，哪些没有价值。即使很少提出引导性问题，访谈仍然会是一个互动的过程。通常情况下，在访谈中，如果新话题的引入次数不超过三四次，访谈者就会发现需要讨论的问题都已经涵盖了。

There are, however, a few ways of phrasing transitions that can prepare respondents for redirection. When it is evident to the interviewer that a particular line of inquiry has been adequately developed, the interviewer might say, perhaps nodding affirmatively, “Okay. Now there is another issue I wanted to ask you about. It is …” The respondent may still be flustered but will have warning that a question requiring reorientation is about to be made.

然而，有一些过渡语的使用方法可以帮助受访者做好重新引导的准备。当面试官意识到某个问题已经得到充分展开时，可以一边点头表示同意，一边说：“好的。现在我想问你另一个问题，那就是……” 受访者可能仍然会有些不知所措，但已经意识到接下来会有一个需要重新调整方向的问题。

How Well Is the Interviewing Partnership Going?

面试合作进展如何？

Be alert to indications by the respondent of discomfort, antagonism, or boredom. If there is any suggestion of any of these, your immediate aim should be to restore an effective partnership. A way of doing this is to listen sympathetically to whatever the respondent wants to offer so long as it is within the study’s frame. Often the respondent will have talked easily and comfortably in an area dealt with earlier in the interview, such as challenges at work and how they were overcome. Returning to that area may improve matters.

密切留意受访者是否表现出不适、敌意或厌倦。如果出现任何此类迹象，您的首要目标应该是重建有效的合作关系。一种方法是，只要受访者的回答不超出研究范围，就耐心倾听他们想要分享的任何内容。通常，受访者在访谈早期涉及的领域，例如工作中的挑战以及如何克服这些挑战，会更容易、更自在地谈论。此时，回到之前的话题或许能改善情况。

Use your own feelings in the interview as a guide to what is going on. If you are being bored by the respondent, something is wrong in the interview. The respondent may be avoiding emotional material or may be defensively providing only superficial elements. Chances are, if the respondent’s account were rich and alive, you wouldn’t be bored.

在访谈中，运用你自身的感受来判断访谈的进展。如果你觉得受访者很无聊，那说明访谈出了问题。受访者可能在回避情感方面的内容，或者出于防御心理，只提供一些表面信息。如果受访者的叙述生动鲜活、内容丰富，你就不会感到无聊了。

Sometimes in an interview I have felt sleepy, almost to the point of being unable to keep my eyes open; the same, I think, has happened to other interviewers. This is boredom to an extreme. Almost never, I believe, is it an indication of fatigue or sleep deprivation. Rather, it suggests that the interview has become lifeless and that the interviewer has bought into an unspoken agreement with the respondent just to get the interview over and done with.

有时在面试过程中，我会感到昏昏欲睡，几乎睁不开眼；我想其他面试官也遇到过这种情况。这其实是极度的无聊。我相信，这种情况几乎从来都不是疲劳或睡眠不足的表现。相反，它表明面试已经变得毫无生气，面试官和受访者之间似乎达成了一种默契，只想尽快结束面试。

If you find boredom with the interview setting in, find a topic with life in it. If the respondent becomes engaged, you will too. There is little value in mechanically plodding on, obtaining still more material that challenges your ability to remain awake. Keep in mind that you are at least as interested in the topics of the interview as a reader of the ultimate report will be. If you are bored by the material, you can be sure its readers will also be bored. The contrary is also the case: if you are fully engaged by the material and drawn in by it so that you feel your understanding is being enlarged by it, then others will be also.

如果访谈过程中你感到有些乏味，那就找一个更有趣的话题。如果受访者投入其中，你也会随之兴致盎然。机械地重复访谈，获取更多让你昏昏欲睡的素材，意义不大。记住，你对访谈主题的兴趣至少要和最终报告的读者一样浓厚。如果你觉得访谈内容枯燥乏味，读者肯定也会感到厌倦。反之亦然：如果你完全沉浸于访谈内容，并从中汲取知识，拓展了理解，那么其他人也会如此。

One approach to finding engaging material, should an interview become boring, is to ask yourself what may be concerning the respondent that the respondent isn’t expressing. If you attend closely, you may pick up clues to emotions underlying the respondent’s account. Respondents may show their emotions in the phrases they use or in the stories they tell or in their posture or voice tone. Should you get a clue about which you feel fairly confident, you might try to check it out—tactfully. A phrasing I use to check out such clues is “It sounds like …” (as in “It sounds like you’re saying that you don’t feel you’ve been properly recognized”). Other introductory phrasings for getting beyond superficials are “Sometimes people who are in situations like the one you’re describing have feelings like …” or “I wonder if you might have been thinking …” But if you’re not comfortable making potentially facilitative comments of this sort, don’t do it. And if you should run into an interview that becomes draggy, do as well as you can with standard techniques and keep in mind that not every interview can be stellar.

如果访谈变得枯燥乏味，寻找引人入胜素材的一个方法是问问自己，受访者可能有什么顾虑而没有表达出来。仔细聆听，你或许能捕捉到受访者叙述背后隐藏的情感线索。受访者可能会通过措辞、讲述的故事、姿态或语气来流露情感。如果你发现了一些比较有把握的线索，不妨委婉地验证一下。我常用的验证方式是“听起来像是……”（例如，“听起来你好像觉得你没有得到应有的重视”）。其他一些能深入挖掘表面信息的开场白包括“有时候，像你描述的这种情况，人们会有这样的感受……”或者“我想知道你当时是不是在想……”。但如果你觉得这类可能起到引导作用的评论不太合适，那就不要说。如果遇到面试拖沓的情况，请尽可能运用标准技巧应对，并记住并非每次面试都能非常成功。

EXAMPLES OF INTERVIEWING

面试示例

EXAMPLES OF GOOD INTERVIEWING

优秀面试的例子

Interview I. Working with a Respondent to Produce Useful Material

访谈一：与受访者合作收集有用材料

Here is an example of effective interviewing, from the study of occupationally successful men. It shows how a good interviewer and a cooperative respondent can work together to produce material useful for a study.

以下是一个有效访谈的案例，该案例来自对职业成功男性的研究。它展示了优秀的访谈者和配合的受访者如何共同努力，获取对研究有用的资料。

The respondent had completed a brief first interview the week before. One aim of this second interview was to learn about stressful incidents at work-how they happened and how they were managed. The interview took place in the respondent’s office.

受访者在前一周已完成一次简短的初次访谈。本次访谈的目的之一是了解工作中遇到的压力事件——这些事件是如何发生的以及如何处理的。访谈在受访者的办公室进行。

This is a description of trying to achieve mastery of self in a situation of what must have seemed catastrophic failure. Note how many leads there are, in this one brief passage, to an understanding of responses to threat. First there is the respondent’s focus on the threat, then his attempt to work out the aims of his enemies, then his disparagement of his enemies together with an effort to reassure himself of his own potency, and finally his protest of the wrong done him.

这段文字描述了在看似灾难性的失败情境中，如何努力掌控自我。请注意，在这短短的一段文字中，蕴含着许多线索，帮助我们理解应对威胁的方式。首先是回应者关注威胁本身，然后是他试图弄清敌人的目的，接着是他对敌人的贬低以及他努力增强自身能力的尝试，最后是他对所受不公的抗议。

The respondent’s reference here to Emmett Franklin was a marker, although the interviewer did not recognize it. Later in the interview, the interviewer asked the respondent how he had managed to maintain himself in the company despite the failure of his presentation to the company’s most important client. At that point the respondent said he had gone to Emmett Franklin and told him that he needed him as a mentor or he would never last. Franklin, who apparently thought well of the respondent, did agree to act as the respondent’s mentor and helped him obtain accounts of his own. But here the respondent discouraged questioning about Emmett Franklin by saying he had never talked with him about the incident and by neglecting to mention that he nevertheless had gone to him for help.

Interview II Negotiating What the Respondent Will Report On

访谈二：协商受访者将报告的内容

Particularly early in a first interview, the interviewer may have to search for the areas in which the respondent can provide useful material. The interview guide will tell the interviewer the areas in which the study needs information, but the respondent may have little to offer in some of the areas, a great deal in others. Or the respondent may feel uncomfortable about reporting material in some areas, and their exploration might be postponed until the interviewing partnership is better established. The following excerpt displays the process of searching, in the beginning of a first interview, for the areas to discuss.

尤其是在首次访谈的初期，访谈者可能需要寻找受访者能够提供有用信息的领域。访谈指南会告知访谈者研究需要信息的领域，但受访者在某些领域可能知之甚少，而在另一些领域则可能有很多信息可以提供。或者，受访者可能对某些领域的信息感到不自在，因此他们的探索可能会被推迟到访谈关系更加融洽之后。以下摘录展示了在首次访谈开始时寻找讨论领域的过程。

The respondent was an IV drug user who had learned a few months before the interview that he was HIV positive. The interview was one of several conducted in a pilot study of reactions among present and former IV drug users to the results of testing for HIV. The interview took place in the HIV clinic of a hospital in which the respondent was an outpatient. The respondent had mentioned, in a brief discussion with the interviewer that preceded the interview, that the medical staff at the hospital were not giving him information he wanted. The interviewer began by asking about this.

受访者是一名静脉注射吸毒者，在访谈前几个月得知自己感染了艾滋病毒。此次访谈是针对当前和曾经的静脉注射吸毒者对艾滋病毒检测结果反应的试点研究的一部分。访谈在受访者就诊的医院的艾滋病门诊进行。在访谈前与访谈员的简短交谈中，受访者提到医院的医务人员没有提供他想要的信息。访谈员首先询问了这个问题。

This is vivid, but it’s hard to know where to go with it. The response suggests both dread of what may happen and discomfort because so much is uncertain. It might be worth learning, perhaps, whether worry about what might happen is always in the respondent’s mind. But the reference to “seeing other people having died from it” sounds like a marker.
